did_you_know.text: Psalm 70 opens with the heading: “For the music director; of David, to bring to remembrance.” The heading identifies the psalm’s connection to David and its purpose as a reminder.
The psalm’s first request is direct and urgent: “God, save me,” and “LORD, hurry to help me.” The word “hurry” expresses a plea for swift action.
The opening verse contains two divine names, “God” and “LORD,” in a single appeal for salvation and help.
The worshiper asks that those seeking his life and desiring his harm be put to shame and disgraced, and that they “turn back”—that is, retreat.
The expression “because of their shame” describes the return of those seeking harm as a result of the disgrace brought upon them.
The words “Aha, aha!” express the mockery or delight of those who desire his harm; the psalm asks that they too be forced to turn back in disgrace.
The psalm contrasts those who desire harm with those who seek God: the former are put to shame and retreat, while those who seek God rejoice and are glad in him.
Those seeking salvation are described as continually saying, “May God be magnified.” Their joy is therefore also connected to an ongoing declaration of God’s greatness.

At the end, the worshiper calls himself “poor and needy” and asks for immediate help. The word “hurry” is repeated from the opening appeal, so the request at both the beginning and the end is for help without delay.
The final verse summarizes the worshiper’s trust: “You are my help and my deliverer.” Alongside his request not to delay, he declares that God is the source of his help and refuge.
